title: The funeral prayer
hook: a prayer said standing, with no bowing and no prostration, and a duty on the whole community

segments.voice: Yesterday: kafan, the shroud, and your line, everyone in white. Today, the community stands before the one in white.

After a regular prayer at the mosque, sometimes the imam turns and says a few quiet words, and people who came only for the noon prayer stay standing. A body, wrapped in white, has been placed at the front. Rows form behind it. And then comes a prayer unlike the others of the day. Nobody bows. Nobody goes down to the ground. The whole prayer happens standing up, and it's over in a few minutes. Some in those rows never met the person, and they are praying for them now.
screen: `A BODY AT THE FRONT.` → `ROWS FORM BEHIND IT.` → `NOBODY BOWS. NOBODY KNEELS.`

segments.voice: It's called salat al-janazah, the funeral prayer. Al-Bukhari keeps a report that shows its shape. When the Negus, the king of Abyssinia, died far away, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, announced his death to the people on the very day it happened. He went out with them to the place of prayer, lined them up in rows, and said Allahu akbar four times. That's the frame: standing, in rows, with four takbirs. In common practice, between them come the opening of the Qur'an, blessings on the Prophet, and du'a for the one who has died, though the schools of law differ on some details. Al-Bukhari also reports that Ibn 'Abbas recited al-Fatiha in a funeral prayer and said he did it so people would know it was the sunnah. Why standing only? One reading is simple: the prayer is for someone else. You stand before Allah on another person's behalf, asking mercy for them. The jurists call it fard kifayah, a communal duty. If some of the community do it, the duty is lifted from the rest; if nobody does, the whole community is at fault. And there's a reward for whoever shows up. In al-Bukhari, the Prophet said, in paraphrase: whoever attends a funeral until the prayer has a qirat, and whoever stays until the burial has two. Someone asked what two qirats were. Like two huge mountains, he said. The person in white can't ask. The community stands for them.
screen: `FOUR TAKBIRS, STANDING, IN ROWS.` · `FATIHA, BLESSINGS, AND DU'A.` · `A COMMUNAL DUTY.` · `TWO QIRATS, LIKE TWO MOUNTAINS.`

segments.voice: Stand up, if you're able, feet planted, hands still, and feel what it's like to stand without any other movement. Think of someone who has died, someone you knew or a stranger whose name you heard, and stay standing for them for a few breaths. If you pray, ask mercy for them in your own words.
Salat al-janazah. The funeral prayer: said standing, with four takbirs, no bowing, a duty the community carries together. Today's word.
Your line: stand for them. Two mountains, for a few minutes on your feet. Peace to you, until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims pray salat al-janazah standing in rows behind the body, with four takbirs and no bowing or prostration, usually reciting al-Fatiha, blessings on the Prophet and a du'a for the deceased; the schools differ on some details.

chat.says: There was a funeral prayer after noon prayer. Do I have to stay if I didn't know them?
options: It's a communal duty, covered if some stay, but staying still earns a qirat.
Yes. Every single person present must stay, or each of them is at fault.
No. The prayer is only for family and close friends of the one who died.
chat.meaning: It's fard kifayah: if some do it, the duty is lifted from the rest. And whoever attends until the prayer has a qirat; until the burial, two.

takbirs.meaning: sayings of Allahu akbar, God is greatest

fard kifayah.meaning: a communal duty: if some do it, the rest are covered

qirat.meaning: a measure of reward, here like a huge mountain

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1245 (the Negus: rows, four takbirs)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1335 (Ibn 'Abbas recited al-Fatiha in the funeral prayer, as sunnah)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1325 (a qirat for the prayer, two for the burial, like two great mountains)

notes: Bukhari 1245, 1325 and 1335 paraphrased; confirm numbers and details.
The order 'Fatiha, blessings on the Prophet, du'a' is given as 'common practice' with a note that schools differ (the Hanafi school does not recite al-Fatiha as such); confirm phrasing.
Fard kifayah is a juristic classification, not stated in the cited hadith; confirm phrasing.
'One reading' of why the prayer is standing only is interpretive; confirm or cut.
Original-language note: جنازة/جِنازة can be voweled janazah or jinazah; confirm.
